newsitem.title: USA: Bulgaria wins IMF cash to back reforms.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria wins IMF cash to back reforms.

text.p: Bulgaria has won $130 million from the International Monetary Fund to back its economic reforms, but an official said on Thursday that the fund was seeking action on banking and structural reform.
"The stability phase has been very rapid," IMF mission chief Anne McGuirk told Reuters, referring to steep falls in monthly inflation after a crisis early this year.
"The main issue is whether they will follow through with the policies needed to deal with the underlying issues in banking and structural reform."

The $130 million, part of a $510 million standby loan, was released after the IMF reviewed the Bulgarian economy on Wednesday. McGuirk said the IMF expected 1997 year-on-year inflation of 566 percent, up from 311 percent in 1996.
But she noted that most of the 1997 inflation was "already behind us" and said monthly inflation was forecast at around two percent for the rest of this year.
Consumer prices rose 0.8 percent in June, down from 5.6 percent in May and 243 percent in February.
The Bulgarian government said in Sofia that the IMF had praised the authorities for their reform efforts.

"The majority of IMF executive directors praised Bulgarian authorities for the restoration of confidence in the national currency and financial institutions, which was more rapid than expected," the government press centre said in a statement.

It added: "The IMF recommended to Bulgaria to follow a more aggressive approach towards the process of liquidation and financial isolation of loss-making enterprises and towards rehabilitation and privatisation of state banks."
Bulgaria's stability efforts have centred on bringing in an IMF-backed currency board, pegging the lev at 1,000 to the mark and backing lev emissions with central bank reserves.
"The currency board is doing very well, better than we expected," McGuirk said. "Interest rates have come down to around six percent for short-term paper, money is flowing back into the system"

She said reserves had risen some $1 billion since April, made up of some $400 million from IMF payments and privatisation receipts and $600 million from people bringing their money back into the system.
The Bulgarian authorities are also seeking to replace the existing $510 million standby arrangement with the IMF with a three-year Enhanced Fund Facility.
The IMF will be looking at evidence that Sofia is building up a track record on reform. "There is a past history of not following through in the structural reforms," McGuirk said.
She said the IMF would look at Bulgaria's economy again in the fall, while a final end-year review would examine Sofia's ability to meet its commitment on the budget and other areas.
"With that kind of reform, I think there would be plenty of support for Bulgaria," McGuirk added.
She said the IMF expected Bulgarian GDP to fall by 7.4 percent this year, after a slump of 10.9 percent last year. But things were looking up for the fragile economy.
"This (fall in output) has largely already happened. We think in the second half of the year they will begin to come out of this trough," she said.
